—My notary. Would an honest man have done such a thing without warning me? Well, it is to prevent you from ruining yourself over a girl that I have come to Paris. When your mother died, she left you enough to live honorably, not enough to lavish gifts on your mistresses.

—I swear to you, Father, Marguerite knew nothing of this gift.

—Then why were you making it?

—Because Marguerite, this woman whom you slander and whom you want me to abandon, is sacrificing everything she possesses in order to live with me.

—And you accept this sacrifice? What kind of man are you, sir, to allow a Mademoiselle Marguerite to sacrifice anything for you? Come now, that is enough. You will leave this woman. A moment ago I was asking you; now I am ordering you. I will have no such filth in my family. Pack your bags and prepare to come with me.

—Forgive me, Father, I then said, but I will not leave.

—Because?...

—Because I have already reached the age when one no longer obeys an order.

My father turned pale at this reply.

—Very well, sir, he resumed; I know what remains for me to do.

He rang.

Joseph appeared.

—Have my bags taken to the Hôtel de Paris, he said to my servant. At the same time, he went into his room, where he finished dressing.

When he reappeared, I went to meet him.

—Will you promise me, Father, I said to him, not to do anything that might cause Marguerite pain?

My father stopped, looked at me disdainfully, and merely replied:

—I believe you are mad.

After which he went out, violently slamming the door behind him.

I went downstairs in my turn, took a cabriolet, and left for Bougival.

Marguerite was waiting for me at the window.




Chapter XXI


—At last! she exclaimed, throwing her arms around my neck. Here you are! How pale you are!

Then I told her about my confrontation with my father.

—Oh, my God! I suspected as much, she said. When Joseph came to tell us of your father’s arrival, I shuddered as though at news of some calamity. Poor darling! And it is I who am causing you all this sorrow. Perhaps you would do better to leave me than to fall out with your father. And yet I have done nothing to him. We are living very quietly, and we are going to live more quietly still. He knows very well that you must have a mistress, and he ought to be happy that it is I, since I love you and desire no more than your position allows. Did you tell him how we have arranged our future?

—Yes, and that is what irritated him most, for he saw in that decision proof of our mutual love.

—What are we to do, then?

—Stay together, my dear Marguerite, and let this storm pass.

—Will it pass?

—It will have to.

—But your father will not leave it at that.

—What do you expect him to do?

—How should I know? Everything a father can do to make his son obey him. He will remind you of my past life and perhaps do me the honor of inventing a few new stories so that you will abandon me.

—You know very well that I love you.

—Yes, but what I also know is that sooner or later one must obey one’s father, and perhaps in the end you will allow yourself to be persuaded.

—No, Marguerite, it is I who will persuade him. It is the gossip of some of his friends that is causing this great anger; but he is good, he is just, and he will reconsider his first impression. Besides, after all, what do I care!

—Do not say that, Armand; I would prefer anything to letting people think that I am making you fall out with your family. Let today pass, and tomorrow go back to Paris. Your father will have reflected on his side, as you have on yours, and perhaps you will understand each other better. Do not clash with his principles; appear to make a few concessions to his wishes; seem not to care quite so much for me, and he will leave things as they are. Have hope, my darling, and be quite certain of one thing: whatever happens, your Marguerite will remain yours.

—Do you swear it to me?

—Do I need to swear it to you?

How sweet it is to let oneself be persuaded by a voice one loves! Marguerite and I spent the whole day repeating our plans to each other, as though we had understood the need to carry them out more quickly. At every moment we expected some event, but fortunately the day passed without bringing anything new.

The next day, I left at ten o’clock and arrived at the hotel around noon.

My father had already gone out.

I went to my own home, where I hoped he might perhaps have gone. No one had come. I went to my notary’s. No one!

I returned to the hotel and waited until six o’clock. Monsieur Duval did not return.

I set out again for Bougival.

I found Marguerite no longer waiting for me as she had the day before, but sitting by the fire, which the season already made necessary.

She was so deeply absorbed in thought that she allowed me to approach her armchair without hearing me and without turning around. When I pressed my lips to her forehead, she started as though the kiss had awakened her with a jolt.

—You frightened me, she said. And your father?

—I did not see him. I do not know what this means. I found him neither at his place nor in any of the places where there was a possibility that he might be.

—Well, you will have to try again tomorrow.

—I am strongly inclined to wait until he sends for me. I believe I have done everything I ought to do.

—No, my darling, that is not enough; you must go back to your father, especially tomorrow.

—Why tomorrow rather than another day?

—Because, said Marguerite, who seemed to blush a little at this question, because your insistence will appear more earnest, and we shall be forgiven sooner as a result.

For the rest of the day, Marguerite was preoccupied, distracted, sad. I was obliged to repeat what I said to her twice in order to obtain an answer. She attributed this preoccupation to the fears for the future inspired in her by the events of the past two days.

I spent the night reassuring her, and the next day she made me leave with an anxious insistence that I could not explain.
